To conceal something means to deliberately hide it — from someone's eyes, from someone's knowledge, or from someone's awareness. When you conceal something, you make sure it is not seen, not found, or not known.

The word works in two directions: hiding something physically (so it can't be seen) and hiding something mentally or informationally (so it can't be known).

She concealed the gift under the bed.
He concealed the truth from his parents.

Both sentences carry the same basic idea — keeping something out of reach of discovery.
The Most Important Feature: It Is Always Deliberate

This is the sharpest and most important thing to understand about "conceal." It is never accidental. When you conceal something, you are making a conscious choice to hide it. There is always intention behind it.

If you forgot to tell someone something, you did not conceal it. But if you chose not to tell them — especially to prevent them from finding out — you concealed it.

This is what makes "conceal" feel slightly more serious and deliberate than a casual word like "hide." It carries a sense of strategy, effort, and purpose.

The word is remarkably flexible. People conceal all kinds of things:

Physical objects — A person can conceal a weapon under their jacket, conceal a letter inside a book, or conceal a key under a doormat. The object is hidden from sight.

Information and facts — A company might conceal its financial losses. A person might conceal their past. A government might conceal evidence. Here, the "hiding" is not physical — it means keeping information from being known or discovered.

Emotions and feelings — This is one of the most common uses. People conceal fear, grief, anger, love, or pain. They don't show it on their face or in their behavior, even though they feel it inside.

She concealed her disappointment behind a smile.

Identity — A person can conceal who they truly are — their real name, their background, their beliefs, or their intentions.

Actions or events — People conceal crimes, mistakes, or affairs. This means they actively work to make sure those things are not discovered.

Concealing does not always mean physically covering something up. It can happen in many ways:

  • By staying silent about something that should be mentioned
  • By lying or telling a half-truth
  • By changing the subject when something gets close to the truth
  • By disguising something so it looks like something else
  • By destroying evidence so nothing can be found
  • By keeping a blank, neutral expression so feelings don't show

All of these are forms of concealment — the common thread is that someone is working to prevent something from being seen or known.

In law: Concealing evidence or concealing a crime is a serious legal offense. It means actively hiding facts that should be disclosed. Courts and legal systems treat concealment as an act of deception with consequences.

In everyday life: People often conceal emotions to be polite, to seem strong, or to protect others from worry. This kind of concealment is very common and not always negative.

In literature and storytelling: Characters frequently conceal their true identity, their secrets, or their motives. This creates mystery, tension, and drama. Many great stories are built around what is being concealed and what happens when it is eventually revealed.

In security and espionage: Agents conceal their identity, conceal information from enemies, or conceal their location. Here, concealing is a strategic act of protection.

Several words are close to "conceal" in meaning, but each has its own shade.

Hide is the most general word. You can hide something without much effort or intention — a child hides behind a curtain during a game. "Conceal" sounds more deliberate, more calculated, and often more serious.

He hid the cookies. (casual, playful)
He concealed the documents from investigators. (serious, intentional)

Disguise means making something look like something else, so it isn't recognized. You disguise something by changing its appearance. Concealing doesn't require a change in appearance — you can conceal something just by keeping it out of sight or out of conversation.

Suppress means stopping something from being expressed or released — you suppress emotions by pushing them down inside yourself. Concealing is broader; it's about hiding from others, whereas suppressing can be something you do even privately, just stopping yourself from feeling or expressing something.

Mask means covering something up so it appears different on the surface — you can mask a bad smell with perfume, or mask nervousness with confidence. "Mask" focuses more on covering the appearance of something, while "conceal" focuses on preventing discovery.

Cover up is the closest informal phrase to "conceal." However, "cover up" often implies a more active or elaborate effort, especially in a negative or scandalous context. You "cover up" a scandal or a crime. "Conceal" is more neutral and can apply to smaller, everyday situations as well.
Sentence Examples to See It in Action

These examples will show you how the word behaves in real usage:

  • The suspect tried to conceal his identity by wearing a hood.
  • She worked hard to conceal her excitement until the right moment.
  • The report revealed that the company had concealed its losses for years.
  • He could not conceal his anger — it showed on his face.
  • The spy carefully concealed the document inside a hollow pen.
  • Doctors discovered she had been concealing symptoms for months.
  • The truth can only be concealed for so long before it comes out.

Notice how naturally the word fits physical hiding, emotional hiding, and informational hiding equally well.

Since you want a complete understanding, here are the other forms of this word:

Concealed (adjective/past tense) — something that has been hidden. "A concealed weapon." "He concealed his past."

Concealing (present participle) — the ongoing act of hiding. "She was concealing her true feelings."

Concealment (noun) — the act or state of hiding something. "The concealment of evidence is a crime."

Concealer (noun) — a person who conceals, or a cosmetic product used to hide blemishes on skin.

The direct opposite of "conceal" is reveal — to make something known or visible that was previously hidden. Other opposites include disclose (formally reveal), expose (reveal something unwanted or hidden), and uncover (discover something that was concealed).
A Final Way to Remember It

If you want one clean mental anchor: to conceal = to keep hidden on purpose.

It can be an object, a feeling, a fact, or an identity. It always involves a choice. And the concealed thing, by definition, is something someone did not want found.
